representations.text:
Your main change was a temporary drop in device-estimated HRV: RMSSD was 22–28 ms on April 3–6, averaging 25 ms versus your 28-day baseline of 44.5 ms. It returned to 43–47 ms on April 7–12. This four-day episode lowered the 14-day average to 39.4 ms (12% lower), rather than representing a sustained decline. It spanned Friday through Monday, so the lower weekend average does not establish a recurring weekend pattern.

Other measures stayed close to baseline during the dip and overall: resting heart rate remained 55–57 bpm; sleep averaged 7h49 versus 7h50, with starts around 22:42–22:58 and waking consistently at 07:00. Steps averaged 8,061 versus 8,054, and low movement 450 versus 448 minutes. Active time eased to 53 from 55 minutes, especially on weekends (51 versus 56), with activity still starting at 21:00. Activity had only a weak relationship with following-night sleep. All measurements were present. Continued recording can show whether the HRV dip recurs; these observations do not explain it.

Your sleep duration increased slightly, while its timing became much less consistent. Across March 30–April 12, recorded sleep averaged 7h58 versus your 28-day baseline of 7h50, with little duration trend. Every successive wake date alternated between 06:30 and 09:00, compared with a consistent 07:00 baseline. Sleep starts likewise alternated between 22:07–22:16 and 00:37–00:44, replacing your baseline 22:43–22:58 range. This continued through both weeks and across weekdays and weekends; an average timing shift would hide that alternation.

Activity still began at 21:00, but the interval between activity ending and sleep starting varied with the sleep schedule. Active minutes had almost no relationship with following-night sleep duration (r=0.07, 13 pairs). Steps rose modestly to 8,052 from 7,940; active time averaged 53 versus 54 minutes and increased slightly through the window, with more on weekends (55 versus 52 weekdays). Low movement stayed near 449 versus 452 minutes. Resting heart rate and RMSSD remained within their baseline ranges, averaging 56.4 bpm and 45 ms. No values were missing. Tracking whether the timing alternation continues would clarify its persistence.

Your sleep changed abruptly late in the window. From March 30–April 6, you recorded 7h54–8h05, slightly longer than your 28-day baseline average of 7h51. On April 7–12, sleep fell to 6h25–6h32, about 82 minutes below baseline, and stayed there through the final weekend without returning. Sleep starts shifted from 22:35–22:46 to 00:08–00:15, while waking remained 07:00. The overall average of 7h21 obscures this six-night change.

Activity also became more variable: six days had 90 minutes at 20:30–22:00, and eight had 45 minutes at 17:30–18:15, versus baseline 50–60 minutes starting at 21:00. Average active time rose 16% to 64 minutes, but shorter sleep followed both schedules. Across 13 correctly aligned pairs, active minutes had almost no relationship with following-night sleep (r=-0.07), so the records do not support attributing the sleep change to activity.

Steps averaged 8,088 versus 7,947; low movement stayed near 449 versus 448 minutes. Resting heart rate and RMSSD remained within baseline ranges, averaging 56.4 bpm and 45.7 ms. All values were present. Continued recording can establish whether the later, shorter sleep persists.

Your recorded sleep was consistently shorter throughout March 30–April 12: 5h35–5h55 every night, averaging 5h46 versus your 28-day baseline of 7h45. That is 118 minutes, or 25%, less per night. Sleep starts moved almost two hours later, from 22:45–23:05 to 00:45–01:05, while waking stayed at 07:00. Sleep lengthened slightly across the window, but never returned to the baseline range. Weekends averaged 5h51 versus 5h44 on weekdays, so the shift persisted across both.

Your other measurements remained comparatively steady: steps averaged 8,037 versus 7,983; active time 55 versus 56 minutes; and low movement 452 versus 450 minutes. Activity continued to start at 21:00 and lasted 50–60 minutes. Its relationship with following-night sleep was negligible in the window (r=-0.08, 13 pairs), compared with a modest inverse baseline relationship (r=-0.36); this does not explain the sleep shift. Device-estimated resting heart rate averaged slightly lower at 55.4 versus 56.1 bpm, and RMSSD stayed near 45 ms. All measurements were present. Continued recording can show whether this persistent later sleep schedule changes.
